paragraphs: Predicting a missing value in a database can require information scattered across several connected tables. Yet many machine-learning benchmarks either treat data as a single table or study graphs without the attributes typical of databases. This paper addresses the gap between those settings, where both table contents and relationships can matter.

The authors explore ways to convert multi-table databases into graphs while preserving their tabular information. They pair these conversions with efficient subsampling and models designed to make predictions from the resulting subgraphs. This creates a framework for examining how the representation of a database interacts with the model trained on it.

The paper also assembles large relational datasets and corresponding prediction tasks. These resources, graph-construction choices, and predictive models come together in the open-source 4DBInfer toolbox. Its main contribution is a shared setting for developing and comparing database prediction methods, helping research move beyond comparisons conducted on disconnected collections of tables or graphs.
neurips-2024-4dbinfer-a-4d-benchmarking-.tldr: 4DBInfer combines relational datasets, prediction tasks, graph construction, and models in a shared toolbox for learning across connected database tables.

paragraphs: Generalized few-shot semantic segmentation asks a model to label image pixels belonging to both familiar categories and new categories learned from very few annotated examples. This makes adding new knowledge only part of the problem: the model must also retain its ability to recognize categories it already learned.

The paper proposes a method built around a simple rule and standard supervised learning. It avoids the customized modules, specially designed losses, meta-learning, and transductive learning used by existing approaches. The authors also provide a theoretical result showing that their method perfectly preserves the original model's segmentation performance for most base classes. That qualification matters: the stated preservation result does not cover every base class.

Experiments support the method's effectiveness. In the one-shot setting, the authors report novel-class segmentation improvements of 6.1% on PASCAL-5i, 4.7% on PASCAL-10i, and 1.0% on COCO-20i. Together, the theoretical and experimental findings show that a comparatively simple learning procedure can improve recognition of new categories while retaining substantial existing capability.
neurips-2024-a-surprisingly-simple-appro.tldr: A simple supervised method improves few-shot segmentation of new categories and theoretically preserves performance for most previously learned categories.

paragraphs: As AI outputs become larger, evaluating them reliably can demand more human attention than is available. This paper studies that problem through goal-conditioned hierarchical reinforcement learning, where decisions have multiple levels of organization. Its central assumption is that people can provide feedback only on outputs smaller than a specified size threshold.

For cardinal feedback, which supplies numerical evaluations, the authors construct a reward for a smaller decision problem and an algorithm that uses low-level feedback to support learning at a larger scale. They establish sublinear regret, meaning that the learning shortfall grows more slowly than the duration of learning within their theoretical setting.

For ordinal feedback, which expresses relative judgments, the authors show that both high-level and low-level feedback are necessary in the setting studied. They develop a hierarchical experimental-design algorithm to gather both efficiently. The contribution is a formal account of when smaller pieces of human feedback can support larger decisions, and how the answer changes with the kind of feedback available.
neurips-2024-a-theoretical-case-study-of.tldr: This theoretical study shows how hierarchical reinforcement learning can use size-limited human feedback, with different requirements for numerical and comparative judgments.

paragraphs: Teaching language models mathematical reasoning often relies on annotated intermediate steps supplied by experts or stronger models. Producing those explanations is costly and labor-intensive. AlphaMath investigates whether a well-pretrained language model can improve its mathematical reasoning by generating its own process-level learning signals through search.

The framework combines the language model with a value model and Monte Carlo Tree Search. Search automatically produces both supervision for reasoning processes and evaluations of individual steps. This gives the system a way to assess possible continuations as it explores solutions, without requiring human-written or GPT-generated annotations of those intermediate reasoning steps.

At inference time, AlphaMath uses step-level beam search guided by the value model. Candidate reasoning paths are therefore assessed using more than the language model's prior probabilities. Experiments on both in-domain and out-of-domain datasets report performance comparable to or better than previous leading methods. The findings support search-generated process supervision as an effective route to improving mathematical reasoning from an already pretrained model.
neurips-2024-alphamath-almost-zero-proce.tldr: AlphaMath uses tree search and a value model to generate mathematical reasoning supervision without human or GPT annotations of intermediate steps.

paragraphs: A high score on a vision-language benchmark does not necessarily show that a model used the image. The authors identify questions answerable from wording, answer choices, or existing world knowledge. They also identify evidence of training-data leakage, where models can answer some questions that should require visual input even when the image is withheld.

These effects can distort estimates of what multimodal training adds. For example, GeminiPro scores 42.7% on MMMU without images. To make evaluation more dependent on visual understanding, the paper introduces MMStar: 1,500 examples spanning six core capabilities and 18 more detailed evaluation axes. An automated selection process is followed by human review for visual dependency, minimal leakage, and demanding multimodal reasoning.

The authors also introduce two metrics for assessing leakage and the performance gain attributable to multimodal training. They evaluate 16 vision-language models on MMStar and use the metrics across seven benchmarks. The contribution combines a curated test set with measurements designed to clarify whether benchmark success reflects actual use of visual information.
neurips-2024-are-we-on-the-right-way-for.tldr: MMStar and two evaluation metrics address image-independent questions and training-data leakage that can inflate apparent vision-language capability.

paragraphs: Topological optimization adjusts data to encourage desired properties of its overall shape. A practical obstacle is that the corresponding loss often responds locally to only a few coordinates. For point clouds, this produces sparse gradients: an optimization step directly tells very few points how to move, making progress slow.

The authors use diffeomorphic interpolation to turn those sparse directions into a smooth, invertible deformation defined throughout the surrounding space. This also works with subsampling. A gradient calculated from a smaller collection of points can determine a deformation that updates the full point cloud, connecting cheaper topological calculations to larger datasets.

The paper applies this idea to latent representations from fixed, black-box autoencoders, without changing their architectures or parameters. Experiments show that a learned deformation can be reused on new latent data in linear time, whereas ordinary topological optimization must run again. Reversing the deformation also lets the authors sample the optimized latent space and map those samples back for generation, supporting greater model interpretability.
neurips-2024-diffeomorphic-interpolation.tldr: Smooth, invertible deformations spread sparse topological gradients across point clouds and can be reused to reshape new autoencoder representations.

paragraphs: Representation learning depends heavily on the data used to train a model, and that dependence can make training expensive. This paper studies what makes data efficient from two perspectives: how it supports optimization during training and how it supports generalization afterward. The emphasis is on improving the usefulness of the training data.

The authors' theoretical and empirical analysis finds that a publicly available prior model can help produce efficient data for a given task. That prior model need not be specific to the target task or architecture. Building on this finding, they introduce the Representation Learning Accelerator, or ReLA, to encourage the creation and use of such data.

In the reported example, a ResNet-18 pretrained on CIFAR-10 informs the training of a ResNet-50 on ImageNet-1K. ReLA reduces computational cost by 50% while matching the accuracy of the original BYOL training procedure. This result demonstrates a concrete case where information from a different pretrained model makes representation learning substantially cheaper without reducing the reported accuracy.
neurips-2024-efficiency-for-free-ideal-d.tldr: ReLA uses a public prior model to make training data more efficient, halving computation in the reported BYOL experiment while maintaining accuracy.

paragraphs: Precise image editing requires finding changes inside a generative model that correspond to understandable visual changes. This paper examines that structure in diffusion models. Within a certain range of noise levels, the authors observe that the posterior mean predictor behaves locally like a linear function and that important directions in its Jacobian occupy low-dimensional semantic subspaces.

The Jacobian describes how small input changes affect the predictor's output. The authors provide theoretical support for the observed local linearity and low-rank structure, then use these properties to build LOCO Edit. The method performs unsupervised, single-step local editing without additional training, using directions identified within the model's semantic subspace.

The identified editing directions exhibit homogeneity, transferability, composability, and linearity, properties that support controllable changes and combinations of edits. The framework also extends to text-to-image models through T-LOCO Edit, supporting unsupervised or text-supervised editing. Experiments demonstrate effectiveness and efficiency, connecting a qualified structural finding about diffusion models to a practical image-editing procedure.
neurips-2024-exploring-low-dimensional-s.tldr: LOCO Edit exploits locally linear, low-dimensional structure in diffusion models to perform controllable image edits without additional training.

paragraphs: Exploration can require accepting a poor result now to make better decisions later. Meta-reinforcement learning aims to learn exploration strategies across episodes, but methods that optimize total reward can struggle with this trade-off. The paper identifies a failure mode where existing methods settle into avoiding exploration because its immediate cost prevents them from discovering its later benefit.

First-Explore addresses this problem by learning two policies with separate roles. One is dedicated to exploration, and the other to exploitation. This separates gathering useful experience from using what has been learned to obtain reward, giving the learning process an explicit way to pursue exploration that sacrifices early performance.

The authors report that First-Explore significantly outperforms existing cumulative-reward meta-learning methods when successful exploration requires foregoing reward in early episodes. The result is specifically about that difficult setting, where short-term incentives can obstruct learning. It supports separating the two policies as a way to learn exploration strategies that existing cumulative-reward methods may fail to acquire.
neurips-2024-first-explore-then-exploit-.tldr: First-Explore learns separate exploration and exploitation policies to handle tasks where early reward must be sacrificed for later success.

paragraphs: Training embodied agents for many tasks is difficult when each task needs a specially designed reward. Language and images offer more natural ways to describe goals, but foundation vision-language models face a substantial gap between their representations and embodied environments. Limited multimodal data in those environments makes adaptation harder.

GenRL connects foundation vision-language representations to the latent space of a generative world model used for reinforcement learning. This alignment requires no language annotations. Tasks supplied through visual prompts, language prompts, or both are connected to the environment's dynamics, and the agent learns corresponding behaviors through imagined experience inside the world model.

Large-scale multitask evaluations in locomotion and manipulation show generalization from both language and visual prompts. The paper also introduces a data-free policy-learning strategy, presenting it as groundwork for broader policy learning with generative world models. The central contribution is a connection between general-purpose multimodal knowledge and models of embodied dynamics, allowing natural task descriptions to guide behavior learning.
neurips-2024-genrl-multimodal-foundation.tldr: GenRL aligns vision-language representations with generative world models so embodied agents can learn tasks specified by images or language.

paragraphs: Imitation learning becomes more complicated when several agents must cooperate. Each agent has local observations and actions, while successful coordination depends on interactions across the group. The resulting state and action spaces are large, and a learning method must connect individual decisions to a shared assessment of team behavior.

The paper extends inverse soft-Q learning to this setting by using mixing networks to combine decentralized Q functions into a joint value function. The local functions capture information associated with individual agents, while their aggregation enables centralized learning. This gives the algorithm a way to represent both individual behavior and collective dependencies within one learning framework.

The authors establish conditions on the mixing networks under which the imitation-learning objective is convex in the space of Q functions. This is a conditional result about that function space. Experiments on challenging multi-agent games, including SMACv2, demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness and support the use of factorized value functions for cooperative imitation.
neurips-2024-inverse-factorized-soft-q-l.tldr: The method combines individual agents' Q functions through mixing networks to enable centralized cooperative imitation learning.

paragraphs: Controllable image generation often depends on annotated conditions such as depth, segmentation, or pose. This paper develops a self-supervised alternative inspired by how visual attributes can become associated without explicit supervision. Its framework, SCG, combines specialized processing modules with a pattern-completion training procedure.

First, a modular autoencoder is trained with an equivariance constraint that encourages independence between modules and correlation within each module. Experiments show specialization for properties including color, brightness, and edges, alongside reported brain-like response features. The specialized modules then provide the basis for learning controllable generation through self-supervised pattern completion.

The authors report that associative generation emerges through this training and generalizes without task-specific training to superresolution, dehazing, and generation conditioned on paintings, sketches, or ancient graffiti. They also find greater robustness than ControlNet in challenging high-noise settings. These results support learning useful visual associations without the same dependence on annotated control datasets, while the self-supervised design offers potential for greater scalability.
neurips-2024-learning-from-pattern-compl.tldr: SCG learns specialized visual modules and pattern completion to enable self-supervised controllable generation with reported zero-shot generalization.

paragraphs: Video restoration benefits from information in neighboring frames, but motion makes that information difficult to combine. Processing contextual frames together can also be computationally expensive. Turtle addresses these issues by maintaining an evolving state that summarizes a truncated history of the video's internal frame representations.

A similarity-based retrieval mechanism selects information from this history while implicitly accounting for motion and alignment between frames. During inference, the causal design allows the model to proceed recurrently, reusing stored historical features. Training can still run in parallel by sampling truncated video clips, so the recurrent inference structure does not require the same sequential processing during training.

The authors report new leading results across tasks including snow and rain removal, super-resolution, deblurring, and blind denoising. They also report lower computational cost than the existing best contextual methods on all evaluated tasks. The findings support a compact historical state as an effective way to retain useful temporal information while reducing the cost of video restoration.
neurips-2024-learning-truncated-causal-h.tldr: Turtle summarizes recent video history in a reusable state, improving restoration results while reducing computation across the reported tasks.

paragraphs: Enhancing a dark image involves more than correcting its overall illumination. Local noise and blur also need attention, and the paper argues that conventional Retinex theory does not adequately address those effects. MambaLLIE is designed to combine broad image context with processing that adapts to local degradation.

Its Local-Enhanced State Space Module adds a local bias to a two-dimensional selective scan, helping preserve spatial dependencies within the image. A second component, the Implicit Retinex-aware Selective Kernel module, selects features through spatially varying operations and adapts its kernel selection to the input. These components are integrated with layer normalization into a global-then-local processing block.

The architecture aims to capture long-range relationships while retaining flexibility in how nearby features are combined. Extensive experiments report significant improvements over leading CNN- and Transformer-based enhancement methods. The stated findings support the combined design for low-light enhancement: broad context helps address illumination degradation, while adaptive local processing handles spatial variation in the image.
neurips-2024-mamballie-implicit-retinex-.tldr: MambaLLIE combines long-range state-space modeling with adaptive local processing to improve low-light image enhancement.

paragraphs: A coordinator learned from demonstrations may reproduce an expert's outcomes when agents follow its recommendations. That does not establish robustness when agents can strategically deviate. This paper separates the value gap, which compares achieved outcomes, from a regret gap that explicitly accounts for opportunities to benefit from deviations.

The difficulty is that strategic behavior can depend on recommendations in situations outside the distribution generated by ordinary coordinated play. Matching demonstrated behavior may therefore leave consequential counterfactual decisions unconstrained. The authors show that value equivalence can coexist with an arbitrarily large regret gap, even though the value gap can be minimized efficiently using extensions of single-agent imitation methods.

To address the harder objective, the paper gives two efficient reductions to no-regret online convex optimization. MALICE requires a coverage assumption on the expert, while BLADES requires access to an expert that can answer queries. These conditions explain what additional support the proposed methods use to learn coordination that accounts for strategic deviations.
neurips-2024-multi-agent-imitation-learn.tldr: Matching an expert coordinator's outcomes can leave large strategic vulnerabilities; minimizing a regret gap requires additional expert coverage or query access.

paragraphs: Language-model recommenders often learn by turning a user's interaction history into a prompt and training the model to produce a positive item. The paper argues that this objective underuses preference information because personalized recommendation also requires distinguishing preferred items from alternatives. Predicting positives alone does not directly express that ranking task.

Softmax-DPO introduces multiple negative items into preference optimization. Its objective adapts direct preference optimization to recommendation by extending a full-ranking Plackett-Luce formulation to partial rankings and connecting it to softmax sampling. This allows training to encode comparisons between preferred items and several alternatives within the recommendation objective.

The theoretical analysis connects the proposed loss to softmax loss with negative sampling and identifies an inherent hard-negative mining benefit: difficult alternatives receive useful attention during learning. Experiments on three real-world datasets show improved preference modeling and recommendation performance, along with better rewards for preferred items. The contribution is an objective that more directly connects language-model training to personalized ranking.
neurips-2024-on-softmax-direct-preferenc.tldr: Softmax-DPO trains language-model recommenders with multiple negative items to incorporate ranking information and improve recommendation performance.

paragraphs: Public pretraining can help differentially private learning, but public and sensitive datasets may differ substantially. This paper asks whether public representations remain useful under that distribution shift. It examines especially difficult cases where both predictions from public data alone and private training from scratch produce unusably weak results.

Across three tasks, the authors find that public features can nevertheless improve private training accuracy by up to 67% over training privately from scratch. This shows that poor zero-shot performance need not mean that the public model's representation is useless for subsequent private learning. Information can remain transferable even when it does not directly solve the target task.

The theoretical explanation depends on public and private data sharing a low-dimensional representation. Under that condition, public representations can reduce the sample complexity of private learning, even when the private task is impossible to learn from public data alone. The results provide empirical and conditional theoretical support for public pretraining under extreme distribution shift.
neurips-2024-on-the-benefits-of-public-r.tldr: Public representations can substantially improve private learning under large distribution shifts, with theory explaining benefits when a low-dimensional representation is shared.

paragraphs: Operator learning aims to learn mappings between spaces of functions, as arise in scientific models based on partial differential equations. This paper studies holomorphic operators between Banach spaces, extending beyond the Hilbert-space setting emphasized in much previous work. The holomorphic restriction defines the class for which its theoretical guarantees are developed.

The method combines approximate encoders and decoders with ordinary feedforward neural networks trained using squared-error loss. The authors identify a network family that achieves optimal generalization bounds. The architectures have constant width exceeding their depth, with dimensions determined by the amount of training data rather than regularity assumptions about the target operator.

For fully connected architectures, the paper establishes that uncountably many training minimizers attain equivalent optimal performance. It also proves that no recovery procedure can improve the generalization bounds beyond logarithmic factors for the problem studied. Numerical experiments on parametric diffusion, Navier-Stokes-Brinkman, and Boussinesq equations illustrate practical performance alongside these theoretical results.
neurips-2024-optimal-deep-learning-of-ho.tldr: The paper establishes near-unimprovable generalization guarantees for neural learning of holomorphic operators between Banach spaces.

paragraphs: An AI character should answer consistently with its entire persona document, including facts unrelated to the immediate question. This paper introduces a precise way to evaluate that requirement. It separates persona statements into active constraints relevant to the query and passive constraints that still must not be contradicted.

The Active-Passive-Constraint score combines statement-to-response inference scores with query-relevance weights. Relevant statements should support the response, while other statements should remain compatible with it. For efficient scoring, the authors distill small, 300-million-parameter inference and relevance models from GPT-4 and report high agreement with GPT-4's judgments.

The score correlates highly with human evaluations on personas containing tens of statements. The authors then use it as a reward system for direct preference optimization, finding that this approach is among the most competitive techniques for satisfying all persona constraints and combines well with other methods. Experiments involving real people with hundreds of statements reach a consistent conclusion, supporting both the evaluation criterion and its use in training.
neurips-2024-quantifying-and-optimizing-.tldr: The APC score measures persona consistency statement by statement and supports preference training that improves faithful role-playing.

paragraphs: Global convolutions can model relationships across long sequences, but learning their kernels is challenging. The kernel must capture distant dependencies while avoiding overfitting. This paper introduces MRConv, a way to parameterize global convolutional kernels so that they can learn expressive long-range patterns across different kinds of data.

MRConv combines convolutions at multiple resolutions, structural reparameterization, and learnable kernel decay. These elements jointly shape how the model represents relationships across sequence positions. The contribution centers on the construction of the convolutional kernel, making long-range convolution more effective as a general-purpose sequence-modeling component.

Experiments report leading performance on Long Range Arena, Sequential CIFAR, and Speech Commands within the comparison class of convolution models and linear-time transformers. The authors also improve ImageNet classification by replacing two-dimensional convolutions with one-dimensional MRConv layers. Together, these findings support the usefulness of the kernel design across several modalities, while the stated leading-performance claim remains tied to the model families and tasks evaluated.
neurips-2024-reparameterized-multi-resol.tldr: MRConv combines multiple resolutions, reparameterization, and learnable decay to improve long-range convolutional modeling across several modalities.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning infers a reward from demonstrations, but a reward that explains observed behavior may fail to capture the task's actual objective. This paper addresses that mismatch within imitation learning. Its focus is on whether the learned policy accomplishes the intended task, beyond fitting the demonstrated behavior.

The proposed semi-supervised framework treats expert demonstrations as weak supervision for deriving a set of candidate reward functions aligned with the task. It then trains a policy against this set through an adversarial mechanism. Using several candidate rewards provides a collective way to assess the policy's ability to complete the task, rather than depending on a single inferred reward.

The authors give theoretical insights into how the framework can mitigate task-reward misalignment and provide a practical implementation. Experiments show improvements over conventional imitation-learning baselines in complex settings and transfer learning. These findings support maintaining and using a set of task-oriented reward candidates when demonstration matching alone produces an inadequate learning objective.
neurips-2024-rethinking-inverse-reinforc.tldr: This imitation-learning framework uses multiple task-aligned reward candidates and adversarial training to reduce mismatch between demonstrated behavior and task objectives.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference can incorporate new evidence by using the previous posterior as the next prior. In practice, this requires an approximation that can be carried forward efficiently. For discrete parameter spaces, the paper identifies a difficulty: strong variational-inference methods can produce approximations that are analytically awkward to reuse in a streaming update.

Streaming Bayes GFlowNets address this problem using learned samplers for discrete compositional objects. A standard GFlowNet first approximates the initial posterior. A specialized update procedure then incorporates each new batch using only the newly observed data, allowing the existing sampler to carry information from earlier inference forward.

Case studies in linear preference learning and phylogenetic inference demonstrate effective sampling from unnormalized posteriors as data arrives. The authors also observe substantial speed gains compared with repeatedly training a GFlowNet from scratch on the full posterior. The contribution is a practical mechanism for updating discrete Bayesian samplers incrementally, reducing the need to repeat the entire learning process after each new batch.
neurips-2024-streaming-bayes-gflownets-9.tldr: Streaming Bayes GFlowNets update discrete posterior samplers using newly arrived data instead of retraining from scratch.

paragraphs: Many facts involve more than two entities, so representing knowledge only as pairs can miss richer relational structure. N-ary knowledge graphs accommodate these multi-entity facts. The paper argues that existing construction methods remain coarse because they often assume a single representation schema and overlook entity order or variation in the number of participating entities.

Text2NKG extracts these relations from text through span-tuple classification. It combines this approach with hetero-ordered merging and output merging to handle relations of different arities. The framework also supports four knowledge-graph schemas: hyper-relational, event-based, role-based, and hypergraph-based representations, broadening the forms in which extracted facts can be organized.

Experiments report state-of-the-art F1 scores on the fine-grained n-ary relation-extraction benchmark. The authors also release their code and datasets. The contribution brings more detailed relation extraction together with flexibility in output structure, supporting knowledge-graph construction when facts vary in how many entities they connect and how those entities participate.
neurips-2024-text2nkg-fine-grained-n-ary.tldr: Text2NKG extracts multi-entity relations of varying arity from text and supports four different knowledge-graph schemas.

paragraphs: Coughing and breathing sounds contain information useful for respiratory health tasks, but collecting large labeled datasets for each application is difficult. This paper explores pretraining on unlabeled respiratory audio as a way to develop reusable models. It also emphasizes openness and reproducibility because the intended application area is safety-critical.

The authors introduce OPERA, a system covering both model pretraining and evaluation. They curate roughly 136,000 respiratory audio samples totaling more than 400 hours, pretrain three foundation models, and assemble a benchmark of 19 downstream respiratory health tasks. This provides shared resources for studying whether specialized pretraining transfers across applications.

The pretrained models outperform existing models trained on general audio on 16 of the 19 tasks. They also demonstrate generalization to unseen datasets and new respiratory audio modalities. These results support the promise of respiratory-specific foundation models and establish an open basis for further research into learning from respiratory sounds when task-specific labeled data is scarce.
neurips-2024-towards-open-respiratory-ac.tldr: OPERA provides open respiratory-audio models and benchmarks, with specialized pretraining outperforming general-audio models on 16 of 19 evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: Conventional denoising diffusion models gradually corrupt data with noise and learn to reverse that process. Generating appealing images can require many reverse steps. UDPM changes the process itself by reducing the latent variable's dimension through downsampling before adding noise, so generation reverses both operations.

The resulting reverse process progressively denoises and upsamples a compact representation into an image. The authors formalize this as a Markovian diffusion process and demonstrate generation on FFHQ, AFHQv2, and CIFAR10. Their approach makes increasing spatial detail part of the generative sequence rather than keeping the latent dimension fixed throughout.

The paper reports generation with as few as three network evaluations, at a combined computational cost below one DDPM or EDM step, alongside an FID score of 6.86. It reports surpassing leading efficient diffusion methods that sample with one denoising step. UDPM also provides an interpretable latent space supporting interpolation, connecting its computational design to more accessible manipulation of the generated image representation.
neurips-2024-udpm-upsampling-diffusion-p.tldr: UDPM combines denoising with progressive upsampling to generate images efficiently from a compact, interpretable latent space.
